claims.text: Local atomic-scale chemical segregation produces heterogeneities in lattice distortion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Heterogeneous lattice distortion reduces local shear moduli.
Regions with reduced local shear modulus promote earlier dislocation nucleation.
Segregation-induced lattice and modulus heterogeneities govern the overall high-temperature thermoelastic and mechanical behavior.
Controlled short-range chemical order can be introduced while all other simulation parameters are held identical.
Short-range chemical segregation causes localized variations in lattice distortion and shear modulus.
Local chemical fluctuations create regions with reduced shear modulus.
Under high temperature and mechanical loading, low-modulus regions nucleate dislocations more readily.
Induced short-range order will broaden the distribution of local shear moduli relative to a homogenized baseline.
Induced short-range order will cause earlier dislocation nucleation relative to a homogenized baseline.
Induced short-range order will produce more pronounced thermoelastic softening under load relative to a homogenized baseline.
A chemically homogenized refractory high-entropy alloy has a uniform thermoelastic response.
A chemically homogenized refractory high-entropy alloy has a higher overall shear modulus than the segregated comparison.
A chemically homogenized refractory high-entropy alloy does not exhibit early dislocation activity.
The magnitude of the predicted effects depends on the parameterization of the simulation method.
Additional microstructural factors omitted from the simulation may affect real-alloy behavior.
